nameStory: This little plant earned its "mouse-ear" name from its fuzzy, oval leaves that are shaped just like tiny mouse ears! The soft, hairy texture of the leaves adds to the resemblance, making you want to reach out and pet them like you would a small animal. The "chickweed" part comes from birds' love of eating the seeds and tender shoots.
description: Common mouse-ear chickweed is a low-growing, mat-forming plant that hugs the ground and spreads outward rather than growing tall. It typically reaches only 4-8 inches in height but can spread widely across the ground by putting down roots wherever its stems touch soil. The plant produces small white flowers and has distinctive fuzzy, tear-shaped leaves that grow in opposite pairs, creating a star-like pattern around the stem.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Soft, fuzzy leaves shaped like teardrops or mouse ears, growing in opposite pairs that create a star pattern around the stem. Run your finger along a leaf - it feels distinctly velvety and hairy.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers with deeply notched petals that look almost split in half, giving each flower a delicate, star-like appearance with what seems like 10 petals instead of 5.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, spreading mats that creep along the ground, rooting wherever stems touch soil. The plant stays low but can cover surprising amounts of ground horizontally.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Hairy stems that feel slightly sticky to the touch and tend to sprawl outward from the center, often rooting at nodes where they contact the ground.

habitat: You'll find common mouse-ear chickweed in disturbed areas like lawns, gardens, roadsides, and waste places throughout New England. It thrives in poor soils and compacted ground where other plants struggle, often appearing in sidewalk cracks, parking lot edges, and overgrazed areas. This adaptable plant tolerates both sun and partial shade.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges early with fresh, bright green fuzzy leaves. Small white flowers begin appearing in late spring and are most noticeable during this season.
seasonality.summer: Continues flowering sporadically through summer while spreading via creeping stems. The mat-like growth becomes most obvious as it colonizes bare patches of ground.
seasonality.fall: Still green and identifiable by its characteristic mouse-ear leaves, though flowering becomes less frequent. The plant remains active later into fall than many other small herbs.
seasonality.winter: Often stays green under snow in milder areas, though growth slows dramatically. Look for the persistent fuzzy leaf rosettes in protected spots.

funFact: This seemingly delicate little plant is actually a botanical escape artist - it can reproduce both by seeds and by cloning itself through creeping stems, allowing a single plant to potentially carpet an entire yard by creating identical copies of itself wherever its stems touch ground!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other chickweeds, but the fuzzy, mouse-ear shaped leaves are the key - common chickweed has smooth, hairless leaves that feel completely different to the touch. Remember: if it's fuzzy like a mouse ear, it's mouse-ear chickweed!
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name including "chickweed," this plant is actually quite different from common chickweed (Stellaria media) and belongs to a different genus entirely. The shared "chickweed" name simply reflects that both plants are favorites of birds and small animals.
compareHints: Among its mouse-ear chickweed relatives, common mouse-ear chickweed is the most widespread and persistent in New England. Field chickweed (Cerastium arvense) has similar flowers but narrower leaves and a more upright growth habit, while sticky mouse-ear chickweed (Cerastium glomeratum) feels noticeably stickier to the touch and has flowers clustered more tightly together.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Snow-in-summer stands out dramatically from its mouse-ear chickweed relatives due to its distinctive 'tomentose' or felty white hairs covering the entire plant, giving it a silvery appearance.
Field chickweed stands out from its mouse-ear relatives by forming the densest, most mat-like growth habit and having the most deeply notched flower petals.
Among the mouse-ear chickweeds in New England, sticky mouse-ear is the only one with that distinctive clammy, tacky feel from its glandular hairs.
American field chickweed differs from other Cerastium species by having the most deeply divided petals - they're split nearly to the base.
Among the mouse-ear chickweeds in New England, common mouse-ear chickweed is the most widespread and has the most consistently fuzzy texture throughout the plant.
Little mouse-ear is smaller and more delicate than common mouse-ear chickweed, which is perennial and has longer petals.
Unlike the very common mouse-ear chickweed which has fuzzy, spoon-shaped leaves and upright flowers, nodding chickweed has narrower leaves and distinctively drooping flowers.
Among its mouse-ear relatives, dwarf mouse-ear stands out for being the tiniest and having petals that don't extend beyond the sepals.
